definition: The Great deluge algorithm (GD) is a generic algorithm applied to optimization problems.
details: It is similar in many ways to the hill-climbing and simulated annealing algorithms. The name comes from the analogy that in a great deluge a person climbing a hill will try to move in any direction that does not get his/her feet wet in the hope of finding a way up as the water level rises. In a typical implementation of the GD, the algorithm starts with a poor approximation, S, of the optimum solution. A numerical value called the badness is computed based on S and it measures how undesirable the initial approximation is. The higher the value of badness the more undesirable is the approximate solution. Another numerical value called the tolerance is calculated based on a number of factors, often including the initial badness. A new approximate solution S' , called a neighbour of S, is calculated based on S. The badness of S' , b' , is computed and compared with the tolerance. If b' is better than tolerance, then the algorithm is recursively restarted with S : = S' , and tolerance := decay(tolerance) where decay is a function that lowers the tolerance (representing a rise in water levels). If b' is worse than tolerance, a different neighbour S* of S is chosen and the process repeated. If all the neighbours of S produce approximate solutions beyond tolerance, then the algorithm is terminated and S is put forward as the best approximate solution obtained.

explainer.lead: The Great deluge algorithm is a search method for finding an approximate solution to an optimization problem. It accepts new candidates while their quality stays within a steadily tightening tolerance, like a climber trying to stay above rising floodwater.

tiers.eli5: Imagine climbing a hill while floodwater rises: you can move to any nearby spot that keeps your feet dry. Here, a solution’s “badness” is like how wet your feet would be, and the allowed water level becomes stricter over time. When no nearby move stays within the limit, you stop and keep the best approximate solution you reached.
tiers.practitioner: Implement it by supplying an initial solution, a badness function, a neighbour generator, an initial tolerance, and a decay function. The tolerance and decay settings control which candidates remain acceptable as the search proceeds. A run ends when every neighbour of the current solution is beyond tolerance, so the result is approximate rather than a guaranteed global optimum.
tiers.paperLevel: Given a solution S, badness b(S), tolerance T, and neighbour set N(S), generate S' in N(S). If b(S') is better than T, set S := S' and T := decay(T), recursively continuing the search; otherwise, try another neighbour. Terminate with S when all neighbours fail the tolerance test, which does not establish global optimality.

explainer.example: Suppose lower badness is better, the current solution S has badness 12, and the tolerance is 10. A neighbour with badness 9 is accepted, so S is replaced and decay lowers the tolerance to 7. If its only neighbours then have badness 10 and 11, both fail the test, and the algorithm returns the solution with badness 9.
explainer.goal: Find an approximate optimum by repeatedly testing neighbouring solutions against a tightening tolerance.
inputs: A badness function for scoring solutions
A way to generate neighbours of S
An initial tolerance and a decay function
steps: Start with a poor approximate solution S and compute its badness.
Calculate an initial tolerance, often using the initial badness.
Generate a neighbouring solution S' and compute its badness b'.
If b' is better than the tolerance, replace S with S' and lower the tolerance using decay.
If b' is worse than the tolerance, keep S and try a different neighbour.
Stop when every neighbour of S is beyond tolerance, and return S.
tradeoffs: The tolerance controls which candidate solutions can be accepted.
Decaying tolerance makes the search progressively more restrictive.
Poor candidates may require many neighbour evaluations before termination.
Stopping after all neighbours fail does not guarantee a global optimum.
